newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian Sorrento coast cut off by fatal landslide.
newsitem.headline: Italian Sorrento coast cut off by fatal landslide.

text.p: The Sorrento peninsula was isolated from the rest of Italy on Saturday after a hillside gave way and at least three people were killed as mud and rock swept down to the sea.

The panoramic coastline, one of southern Italy's biggest holiday draws, was inaccessible by land from Naples as emergency workers battled to clear 10,000 cubic metres (400,000 cu ft) of earth and stone dumped on the winding coast road.
"I heard an enormous roar and the next thing I saw was a huge chunk of the coast collapse," policeman Guglielmo Pignataro said.

Two houses were wrecked and several cars buried or swept into the sea in the landslide on Friday night. It occurred near the village of Pozzano, at the southern end of the Bay of Naples, after two days of torrential rain.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano said the government would declare the area, accessible only by sea, a disaster zone.
The fire service put the casualty toll at three dead and 20 injured. At least one person, a woman of 83, was missing.

Divers scoured waters off the coast for any bodies trapped in vehicles as more heavy rain battered the peninsula, whose terraced hills of lemon and olive groves and vineyards plunge straight down to the sea.
Other landslides closed scores of roads throughout the Naples region. In the city itself, transport officials said they had halted the local funicular railway as a precaution.
Naples and the surrounding region, dominated by the Mount Vesuvius volcano, is one of the most susceptible areas to earthquakes, landslides and other natural disasters in Italy.
Flood-related disasters have killed 350 people there in the last 50 years, including 297 in 1954, when 205 of the victims were on the Sorrento peninsula alone.
The latest deaths prompted fresh calls for national action to halt soil erosion, much of which is blamed on illegal building and land clearances.
"The land has been under attack for decades. It has been plundered and destroyed," the mayor of Naples, Antonio Bassolino, told reporters.

Villagers in Pozzano said they believed nearby rock-blasting last summer to build a road tunnel, work on which has since been stopped, may have played a part in the accident. The theory was likely to figure in a formal investigation by magistrates.
Environment Minister Edo Ronchi said 65 percent of Italy's land mass was at risk of water-related slippage and erosion but that much of the risk could be prevented with proper action.
"In the past 30 years, erosion-related disasters have killed 3,000 people and 35 trillion lire ($22 billion) has been spent on coping with these catastrophes. This is the result," he said.
